results.title: What to do if your job makes you sick
results.description: Who has not felt, on some occasion, that work makes them sick? Or that a tyrannical superior gives them hives? Sanguine, the film with which French director Marion Le Corroller won the latest edition of the Sitges Festival, responds to these questions with a fable-like tone that combines, somewhat unsteadily, body horror and social satire. Placing itself in a genealogical line with the cinema of Julia Ducournau (Raw) and Coralie Fargeat (The Substance), what distinguishes Sanguine from this new wave of feminist body horror is its theme, which moves away from the female experience to address concerns of generational scope.

results.title: Britain can now sanction war criminals - could Sri Lanka's commanders be next?
results.description: Britain can now sanction war criminals - could Sri Lanka's commanders be next? by Thusi test Wed, 25/11/2026 - 14:32 Body The UK Foreign Secretary, Ed Miliband, who announced the new powers in September. Photograph: UK Government / OGL Britain can now sanction individuals and entities for war crimes for the first time, after Parliament approved an expanded human rights sanctions regime that covers serious violations of international humanitarian law and the obstruction of humanitarian aid, powers that could be used against Sri Lankan commanders accused of atrocities against Tamils. The Global Human Rights and International Humanitarian Law Sanctions Regulations 2026 replace the regime introduced in 2020, which allowed sanctions only for serious violations of the right to life, freedom from torture and freedom from slavery and forced labour. The new rules add three grounds: serious violations of international humanitarian law, obstruction of the delivery of or access to humanitarian assistance, and serious violations of the right to liberty and security of person. The regulations came into force on 15 October and were approved by Parliament on 4 November, Human Rights Watch said. The House of Lords approved them while also passing a motion to regret. They also allow the government to designate a whole class of people by description, such as all members of an organisation that is itself sanctioned, according to an analysis by REDRESS. The UK Foreign Secretary, Ed Miliband, first announced the change in September as part of measures against Israel's settlement expansion in the West Bank. Human Rights Watch called it “an important step that means the UK can impose consequences for atrocities committed around the world”, while stressing that sanctions must not replace criminal prosecutions. “It is important that such sanctions are treated distinctly from criminal accountability,” the organisation said. “Accountability for international criminal acts, past or present, should be implemented through criminal justice, including fair trials.” First use Britain has already used the new powers twice this month. On 17 November it sanctioned eight Israeli settlement builders and the activist group Tzav 9 for blocking aid convoys to Gaza, citing serious violations of international humanitarian law. On 23 November, alongside its formal recognition of the Rohingya genocide, it designated a Myanmar brigadier general under the new regime over the treatment of prisoners in Chin State. Sri Lanka's commanders In March 2025, Britain used the old regime to sanction four Sri Lankans: the former armed forces head Shavendra Silva, former navy commander Wasantha Karannagoda, former army commander Jagath Jayasuriya and paramilitary leader Karuna. They were designated for serious human rights violations including extrajudicial killings, torture and sexual violence. Shavendra Silva, one of four Sri Lankans sanctioned by the UK in March 2025. File photograph The new grounds go to the heart of the accusations against the Sri Lankan state over the genocide of 2009. UN investigations have found reasonable grounds to believe that Sri Lankan forces repeatedly shelled hospitals and the government-declared No Fire Zones where hundreds of thousands of Tamils were trapped, and that the government severely restricted food and medicine to the Vanni, conduct that may amount to war crimes. Until now, the shelling of hospitals and the denial of humanitarian aid fell outside the scope of Britain's human rights sanctions. Human Rights Watch urged Britain to apply the regime “in a principled and consistent manner” and to ensure its own courts can prosecute war crimes “wherever they occur and whoever commits them”.
